title: Mechatronics and Robotics
description: Microcontrollers, sensors, motors and drivers, state machines and the geometry of robot arms and wheeled robots.
audience: Adults who finished Electronics Foundations and know basic programming; no hardware experience needed.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a microcontroller's timing and I/O.
You'll be able to convert sensor readings to physical units.
You'll be able to size a motor drive.
You'll be able to compute arm and wheeled-robot kinematics.

sources.title: Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control (Cambridge, 2017)
sources.licence: Free preprint PDF; copyright Cambridge University Press

sources.title: Arduino documentation (language reference, hardware pages); concepts only

lessons.title: What a microcontroller is
lessons.objective: Describe the parts of a microcontroller and compute clock and timer timings.

concepts.title: Microcontroller
concepts.summary: A single chip holding a processor, memory and peripherals such as pins, timers and converters, built to read inputs and drive outputs.

concepts.title: Timer
concepts.summary: A counter driven by the clock, optionally slowed by a prescaler, that overflows at a known interval.

misconceptions: Learners think a microcontroller is a small PC. It has no operating system by default and runs one program forever.
Learners think faster clock always means better; power and I/O matter more.
Learners think delay() is free; the processor does nothing else while waiting.
sequence: Read, decide, act, repeat.
CPU, flash, RAM, pins.
Clock and cycles.
Timer with prescaler.
Peripherals do work without the CPU.

examples: 16 MHz clock: 62.5 ns per cycle.
Prescaler 64: tick 4 microseconds; an 8-bit timer overflows after 256*4=1.024 ms.
A loop of 2000 cycles at 16 MHz runs 8000 times per second.

lessons.title: Analog signals and the converter
lessons.objective: Convert between voltage and ADC counts and recover a sensor value through a divider.

concepts.title: ADC
concepts.summary: Converts a voltage to an integer of 2^n levels; one step (LSB) is Vref/2^n.

concepts.title: Divider sensing
concepts.summary: A resistive sensor in a divider turns resistance into voltage.

misconceptions: Learners treat the reading as the voltage itself.
Learners think more bits means more accuracy; accuracy depends on references and noise.
Learners think averaging cures all noise; it only reduces random noise by sqrt N.
sequence: Quantisation.
LSB = Vref/2^n.
Count to voltage.
Divider and thermistor.

concepts.summary: Two out-of-phase channels give direction and four counts per pulse cycle.

concepts.title: Time of flight
concepts.summary: Distance is half of speed times round-trip time.

misconceptions: Learners confuse encoder pulses per revolution with counts per revolution.
Learners forget the halving for echo.
Learners think sensors give truth; they have resolution, noise and drift.

lessons.title: State machines
lessons.objective: Read and design a finite state machine and write it without blocking delays.

concepts.title: Finite state machine
concepts.summary: A set of states, events and a table saying which state follows each event.

concepts.title: Non-blocking timing
concepts.summary: Check elapsed time each pass instead of waiting.

misconceptions: Learners write behaviour as nested if statements on flags; the flags drift out of step. One state variable cannot.
Learners think every state must handle every event. Unlisted pairs should do nothing, and that must be a decision.
Learners use delay() for a pause and then miss a button press during it.
sequence: Start with a vending machine or door: behaviour depends on what already happened, not only on the input.
Name the states and the events that move between them.
Write the transition table; blank cells mean stay put.
Turn the table into code: one state variable, one lookup per event.
Replace delay() with elapsed-time checks so events are never missed.
Add a safe state that every fault event leads to.
examples: Table idle,run,pause traced with events.
4 states and 3 events give at most 12 transitions.
Traffic light cycle.

Learners think a stalled motor is safe; it overheats.
Learners confuse rpm and rad/s.

lessons.title: Steppers and servos
lessons.objective: Compute step counts, speeds and positions for steppers and hobby servos.

concepts.title: Stepper motor
concepts.summary: Moves in fixed angular steps, 1.8 degrees for 200 steps per revolution.

concepts.title: Servo
concepts.summary: A motor with position feedback; a hobby servo reads a 1 to 2 ms pulse every 20 ms.

misconceptions: Learners think steppers cannot lose steps; overload or too-fast acceleration makes them skip silently.
Learners think 16x microstepping gives 16x accuracy; it gives finer commands, not equal accuracy.
Learners think servo pulse width sets speed; it sets position.
sequence: Coils pull a toothed rotor one step at a time: 200 steps is 1.8 degrees.
Position is counted, not measured, so it is open loop and loses steps if overloaded.
Microstepping shares coil current to make smaller steps, with less torque gain per step than the count suggests.
A lead screw turns steps into linear distance: lead / steps per rev.
A hobby servo hides a motor, gearbox, potentiometer and a feedback loop; pulse width commands angle.
Choose a stepper for repeatable positioning at modest load, a servo for compact closed-loop angle.
examples: 200 steps/rev x16=3200; 600 rpm full steps: 2000 steps/s.
1.25 ms pulse = 45 degrees.

lessons.title: Sizing a motor and gearbox
lessons.objective: Find wheel torque and speed for a robot and choose a gear ratio.

concepts.title: Wheel torque
concepts.summary: Force at the ground times wheel radius.

concepts.title: Reflected torque
concepts.summary: Motor torque needed = wheel torque / (ratio x efficiency).

misconceptions: Learners size for speed only and then find the robot cannot climb a ramp.
Learners forget gearbox efficiency, so the motor is undersized by a fifth or more.
Learners use the total force on one wheel instead of sharing it across driven wheels.
sequence: State the job: robot mass, steepest slope, top speed, wheel radius.
Force along the slope: m g sin(angle); split across driven wheels.
Wheel torque = force x radius.
Wheel speed from v / r; ratio = motor speed / wheel speed.
Motor torque = wheel torque / (ratio x efficiency).
Add a margin of about 2x and check stall current against the driver.
examples: 6 kg on 10 degrees: 10.22 N, 5.11 N per wheel, 0.256 N m at r=0.05.
0.5 m/s: wheel 10 rad/s=95.5 rpm; motor 3000 rpm gives about 31:1.
At 30:1, 80 percent: motor torque 10.6 mN m.

lessons.title: Arms: where is the hand?
lessons.objective: Compute the end position of a two-link arm and its reach.

concepts.title: Forward kinematics
concepts.summary: The tool position follows from the joint angles and link lengths.

concepts.title: Workspace
concepts.summary: The set of points the tool can reach; for two links it is a ring.

misconceptions: Learners use t2 alone for the second link instead of t1+t2.
Learners think the workspace is a full disc; a short second link leaves a hole in the middle.
Learners confuse joint angles (relative) with world angles (absolute).
sequence: Draw a base frame and a two-link arm with joint angles measured from the previous link.
The elbow position is (l1 cos t1, l1 sin t1).
The hand adds (l2 cos(t1+t2), l2 sin(t1+t2)); angles add.
Reach is largest when straight (l1+l2) and smallest when folded (|l1-l2|).
So the workspace is a ring, not a disc.
Real joint limits trim the ring.
examples: Workspace ring 0.1 to 0.5 m.
Full stretch reach 0.5.

lessons.title: Inverse kinematics
lessons.objective: Find joint angles for a target point and see why there are two solutions.

concepts.title: Inverse kinematics
concepts.summary: Finding joint angles for a given tool position.

concepts.title: Elbow configurations
concepts.summary: Two solutions mirror each other, up and down.

misconceptions: Learners think there is one answer; there are usually two.
Learners use arctan(y/x) alone for t1, ignoring the second link.
Learners do not check reach before solving and take acos of a number above 1.
sequence: Ask the reverse question: which angles put the hand at (x, y)?
Law of cosines on the triangle of l1, l2 and the line to the target gives cos t2.
Two signs of t2 give two arms, elbow-down and elbow-up.
Find t1 from the target direction minus the offset the second link causes.
At full stretch the two solutions merge; velocities become impossible (a singularity).
Pick the solution by joint limits and the shorter move.
examples: Target (0.35,0.20): cos theta2=0.2708, theta2=74.29 degrees.
theta1=29.74-28.53=1.22 degrees for elbow-down; 58.27 for elbow-up.
A target at 0.6 m is unreachable.

lessons.title: Mobile robots and sensor fusion
lessons.objective: Compute differential-drive motion and blend gyro and accelerometer data.

concepts.title: Differential drive
concepts.summary: v = (vr+vl)/2 and w = (vr-vl)/L.

concepts.title: Complementary filter
concepts.summary: Combines gyro (good short term) and accelerometer (good long term).

misconceptions: Learners think odometry stays accurate; error only grows.
Learners average two sensors equally, ignoring that their errors have different timescales.
Learners think a gyro measures angle; it measures rate and must be integrated.
sequence: Two driven wheels set forward speed (average) and turn rate (difference over track).
Integrate speed and turn rate each step to update the pose: odometry.
Small errors in wheel diameter and slip accumulate: drift.
A gyro measures turn rate, smooth but drifting; an accelerometer gives a noisy absolute tilt.
Blend: angle = a(angle + gyro dt) + (1-a) accel.
A Kalman filter picks the blend by modelled uncertainty; the complementary filter fixes it.
examples: A 1 degree heading error grows to 1.7 cm over 1 m.

lessons.title: Putting a robot together
lessons.objective: Organise sensing, decision and action in time, power and safety.

concepts.title: Sense-plan-act loop
concepts.summary: A repeating cycle with a fixed period.

concepts.title: Power budget
concepts.summary: Battery energy divided by average power gives run time.

misconceptions: Learners budget average current and then brown out on motor start-up peaks.
Learners run everything in one loop at one rate, so a slow sensor read delays motor control.
Learners design driving but not stopping.
sequence: Split the robot into sensing, deciding and acting layers.
Give each a rate: motor control fast (100 Hz or more), distance sensors slower, planning slowest.
Express behaviour as a state machine of simple modes (search, approach, avoid, stop).
Tally current for every part to find peak and average power.
Divide battery energy by average power for run time, and size wiring and driver for the peak.
Define a safe state, an emergency stop and a watchdog before the first run.
examples: 2000 mAh at 7.4 V=14.8 Wh; 12 W average gives 1.23 h.
Control 100 Hz, sensors 20 Hz.
Watchdog resets a hung loop.

platformNeeds: A two-link arm kinematics explorer with draggable joints and target.
A microcontroller pin/timing simulator is not required; svg_figure suffices.
